agenda: Review Q3 retention, ETA accuracy, and onboarding results against the goals for Kestrel Dispatch.
Choose the Q4 product bets and settle the disagreement about self-serve onboarding.
Define the driver mobile app v2 release and the ETA model's safety gates.
Size engineering capacity, budget, and two backend hires.
Align customer communication, launch marketing, risks, owners, and dates.

chapters.title: Opening and Q3 Scorecard
beats: Priya frames Q4 as a choice among three bets, not a list of every requested feature.
Amara explains 4.1% churn and customers taking 19 days to onboard; Daniel connects those numbers to lost sales momentum.
Lucas clarifies that ETA accuracy is 82% under a ten-minute arrival window and weak on weekend freight lanes.

chapters.title: Customer Needs and the Three Bets
beats: Daniel makes the case for a dependable driver app; Amara argues onboarding needs a Q4 answer.
Jonas describes app v2 as fewer driver steps, offline clarity, and a reliable stop list rather than a visual refresh.
Priya proposes mobile v2, an ETA-accuracy model, and staged self-serve onboarding as the three bets.

chapters.title: Mobile App v2 Scope and Release Gates
beats: Jonas and Mei debate swipe-to-complete against an explicit confirmation control and agree to validate both with drivers.
Mei limits the first release to onboarding, stop list, offline queue, and safer completion; Lucas specifies event tracking.
Hannah and Amara require a carrier pilot before launch claims, with crash-free sessions and sync success as gates.

chapters.title: ETA Accuracy Model and Evidence
beats: Lucas proposes moving ETA accuracy from 82% to 88% without worsening weekend lanes.
Amara challenges a broad accuracy claim with the Harlan Freight escalation and a 42-truck carrier's long misses.
Mei and Lucas settle on shadow evaluation, segment reporting, and a rollback path before production.

chapters.title: Self-Serve Onboarding Decision
beats: Mei argues for cutting self-serve to protect the mobile app and the platform team's workload.
Daniel and Amara explain why a 19-day onboarding cycle damages conversion and early retention.
Priya resolves the disagreement with a narrow, gated self-serve pilot: imports, field mapping, and assisted review, without general availability in Q4.

chapters.title: Capacity, Budget, and Hiring
beats: Mei sizes the quarter at 30 effective engineering weeks after operations, holidays, and support load.
Omar challenges the cost of two backend hires and a broad launch budget; Mei explains the platform bottleneck.
The group approves two backend requisitions within a capped budget and stages spending against milestones.

chapters.title: Launch, Customer Communication, and Risks
beats: Hannah separates an October pilot message from a later public app launch and asks for evidence behind every claim.
Amara sets customer communication needs around delays, offline use, and onboarding expectations.
Priya assigns owners for risk tracking, launch readiness, sales enablement, and customer pilot recruitment.

chapters.title: Decisions, Owners, and Close
beats: Priya restates the three bets and the self-serve pilot boundary.
Each owner confirms a concrete next step and spoken due date.
The team closes with a shared decision log and a review cadence.
